entities.summary:
Protagoras (c. 490 BCE – c. 420 BCE), a foundational figure of the Greek Sophistic movement, radically reshaped philosophical inquiry in 5th-century BCE Athens by positing 'man is the measure of all things.' His bold assertion challenged traditional notions of objective truth and divine authority, making human perception and convention the arbiters of knowledge and ethics. Operating during the intellectual ferment of Periclean Athens, Protagoras became the first to professionalize philosophical instruction, commanding significant fees for teaching rhetoric and civic virtue to aspiring statesmen and citizens, thereby directly influencing the intellectual climate that produced figures like Socrates and Plato, even as they critiqued him.

Born in Abdera, Thrace, Protagoras traveled widely throughout the Greek world, eventually settling in Athens where he gained renown as a teacher and orator. His most famous dictum, 'Man is the measure of all things: of things that are, that they are; of things that are not, that they are not,' profoundly impacted epistemology, shifting philosophical focus from cosmic speculation to human experience. He developed the 'antilogical' method, arguing that two opposing arguments could be made for every proposition, a technique central to his rhetorical instruction. Protagoras taught *aretē* (virtue or excellence) and *technē* (skill), particularly in persuasive speech, to young Athenians eager for political success, attracting students with his promise of practical wisdom and effective argumentation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Protagoras fundamentally shifted philosophical inquiry from cosmology to human-centered questions of knowledge and ethics, influencing the development of Western philosophy and rhetoric through his innovations in education and his challenge to objective truth. His ideas directly provoked figures like Plato and Aristotle to formulate their own theories of reality and knowledge.
